lines: STAFF REPORT C ITY OF OCEANSIDE
DATE: May 9, 2024
TO: Chairperson and Members of the Housing Commission
FROM: Housing & Neighborhood Services Department
SUBJECT: 2024 AFFORDABLE HOUSING NOFA FUNDING RECOMMENDATION
SYNOPSIS
Staff recommends that the Housing Commission recommend that the City Council of
the City of Oceanside and the Community Development Commission
1. A uthorize the expenditure of HOME-ARP, Low/Mod Income Housing Asset, and
Inclusionary Housing In-lieu Fee funds in fulfillment of the 2024 Notice of Funding
Availability (NOFA);
2. Approve the conditional award of funding in the form of a residual receipts loan in
the amount of $4,250,000 and forty -three (43) federal Project Based Housing
Vouchers (PBVs) and twelve (12) Veteran Affairs Supportive Housing (VASH)
Vouchers for the development and operation of a 56- unit affordable senior
housing community at 1111 and 1123 South Coast Highway and $6,000,000 and
fifty (50) PBVs for the development and operation of a 111- unit affordable
housing community at 2136 South El Camino Real; and
3. A ppropriating funds thereof.
BACKGROUND
The City of Oceanside is committed to creating and maintaining housing that is
affordable to Oceanside’s residents and workforce, including lower -income individuals,
as well as families and older adults, and community members currently or formerly
experiencing homelessness. To support the efforts of affordable housing developers to
address the housing needs of the Oceanside community , on February 28, 2024, the
City issued a Notice of Funding Availability (2024 NOFA) for development or
preservation of affordable housing (Attachment 1) . The application period ended at
4:00PM on March 22, 2024, with five responses received. Staff reviewed the responses
and confirmed all projects meet the requirements for consideration for funding. A panel
of housing staff of various cities and Oceanside city staff reviewed the five responses
and assisted in the development of the funding recommendation provided in this report
for consideration by the City Council.
ANALYSIS
The City maintains a number of funding sources to assist in the development of
housing programs and opportunities to address the various housing needs of the
community, from rehabilitation of housing, rental assistance, homeless programs and
services and development of new affordable housing. The City periodically issues a
NOFA to receive responses and evaluate the needs of sponsors seeking funding from
the City for the development and preservation of affordable housing.
Presently, the City has the following available funding sources, with each fund
summarized below.
1. Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund. The Inclusionary Housing In-lieu Fee
Fund receives monies paid by developers of market -rate housing subject to the
City’s affordable housing requirements of Chapter 14C of the Oceanside City
Code (OCC) in-lieu of including affordable housing in a residential project. The
Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund has a current balance of $14 million.
2. Oceanside Successor Agency Low/Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund
(LMIHF). On February 1, 2012, the State Legislature enacted AB 26, which
dissolved all California Redevelopment Agencies and provided for Successor
Agencies to assume the rights, powers, and duties of the former redevelopment
agencies. The City of Oceanside is the Successor Agency to the former
Oceanside Redevelopment Agency, and the City Council acts as the governing
board of the Successor Agency. Remaining LMIHF are available exclusively for
the preservation, improvement, and expansion of the low - and moderate-income
housing supply within the community. Statutory obligations require that over each
five-year compliance period, at least 30 percent of such development
expenditures must assist extremely low-income households at 30 percent or less
of the Area Median Income (AMI), while no more than 20 percent may assist low -
income households between 60 to 80 percent of AMI. Currently, the LMIHF has a
balance of $2.8 million.
3. HOME Funding. The City of Oceanside i s a HOME Investment Partnership
Program (HOME) entitlement jurisdiction and receives an annual award of HOME
funds from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). The
goal of the HOME program is to provide funds to expand the supply of affordable
housing for very low-income and low-income persons as defined under 24 CFR
92. Expenditures must primarily benefit households at 60 percent of the AMI. As
a HOME entitlement jurisdiction, Oceanside receives an annual HOME entitlement
of approximately $460,000. HOME funds must be committed within 24-months of
the award date.
HOME-A RP funding was provided as a one- time source of funding under the
American Rescue Plan Act of 2021. These funds support the development of
permanent housing units for individuals experiencing or at risk of homelessness
and are subject to 24 CFR 92 and/or HOME-ARP Program Requirements. HOME-
ARP funds were awarded in August 2022 for a total of $2,248,491, of which
$1,911,217 is available for eligible housing activities and must be expended by
September 2030.
4. Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA) Funding. Senate Bill 2 (SB2),
adopted in 2017, established a permanent source of funding, Permanent Local
Housing Allocation (PLHA), intended to increase the affordable housing stock in
California. Oceanside is eligible to apply for non- competitive, PLHA entitlement
funds from the State of California (“State”) Department of Housing and
Community Development (HCD) . The current five-year plan covering funding
available through Calendar Year (CY) 2025 allocates funds to the development and
operation of the Oceanside Navigation Center . The PLHA Five -Year Plan would
need to be amended to provide funding for acquisition, predevelopment,
development, and preservation of multi-family projects or permanent or transitional
housing, with an emphasis on projects for households that are at or under 60
percent AMI. Funding available as an entitlement community is approximately
$2,675,850, with funds to be used for reimbursement of any eligible expenses to the
Inclusionary Housing In-Lieu Fee fund and the City’s share of operational costs of
the Navigation Center.
5. Project Based Vouchers (PBV). The Oceanside Housing Authority (OHA)
administers the federal “Section 8” Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program and
HUD Veteran Affairs Supportive Housing (VASH) vouchers for homeless
veterans. The OHA may make available up to 20 percent of the amount of
budget authority allocated to the OHA for Project Based Housing Voucher (PBV)
assistance. The OHA has a balance of approximately 183 PBV authority to
provide as a subsidy for new -construction, multi -family rental housing
developments serving qualified, very low-income, and special needs households
with incomes at or below fifty percent (50%) AMI.
2024 NOFA – Affordable Housing
On February 9, 2024 , the City’s Housing and Neighborhood Services Department
issued a Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA) for the acquisition/rehabilitation or new
development of 100 percent affordable rental housing projects in the approximate
amount of six million dollars ($6,000,000), along with approximately fifty (50) PBVs and
up to thirty (30) VASH PBVs based upon a consultation and recommendation of the
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). Qualified affordable housing sponsors were
invited to submit requests for funding for construction or preservation of affordable
rental housing for seniors, families, and individuals and families with special needs
including individuals and families who formerly experienced homelessness. The NOFA
allows the City Council to authorize additional funding above the published $6,0 00,000
amount and PBVs at its discretion. The application deadline for this NOFA was March
The NOFA provided the following considerations for awarding funding:
 M eets all requirements provided in the NOFA
 Project Approach and Concept
o Creation of new affordable housing units;
o Serves a special needs group (e.g. seniors, persons with disabilities, large
families, or serve very low - and/or extremely low -income households,
unsheltered or at -risk of homelessness, or include 20 percent or more
permanent supportive housing);
o Requesting a minimum of ten percent (10%) of the PBVs as HUD-VASH;
o Overall project concepts, layout, extent of neighborhood enhancement, and
incorporates community spaces and amenities;
o Number of affordable units, A rea Median Income (AMI) levels, target
populations, supportive service plans for the target population;
o Includes provision of supportive housing units;
o Evidence of site control;
o Extent to which project meets or maximizes base density;
o Location near major transit stop and a very low VMT areas, near amenities or
neighborhood services;
o Location within high opportunity areas of the City; and,
o Project readiness, including, but not limited to, possessing complete project
entitlements and permits or timeline and probability of obtaining necessary
approvals based on the proposed project’s design and regulatory constraints,
with an overall project schedule for delivery of affordable units within three
years.
 Financial Feasibility, within an expedited manner
o Amount of NOFA funding request , reasonable public subsidy and maximizes
investment;
o Competitive p roject proforma, including reasonable cost s, operating
income/expenses, and underwriting assumptions;
o Leveraged project financing plan that includes a variety of public and private
capital funding sources; and,
o Cash flow projections demonstrating that the proposed project, once
operational, will meet all debt service or other operational expense obligations
for a minimum period of 20 years.
 Developer Capacity
o Developer capacity to perform and to oversee the work necessary for
successful completion of the proposed development;
o At least one member of the developer team must have completed at least one
affordable housing project within the City of Oceanside or a comparative
locality;
o Exhibit prior work resulting in successful development of affordable rental or
permanent supportive housing; and,
o Development team’s experience and ability to deliver high quality services to
the target resident population.
The City received f ive (5) responses to the NOFA totaling $25,071,000, with the new
construction of 403 units and the extension of the affordability period of an existing 144
units through acquisition and rehabilitation. The five proposals received are summarized

A copy of the full applications submitted in response to the 2024 NOFA are available in
the Housing & Neighborhood Services Department during normal business hours , due
to the substantial length of the documents.
In March 2024, the Housing & Neighborhood Services Department assembled a panel
of housing staff from the jurisdictions of San Marcos, Vista, Carlsbad, and El Cajon,
along with City staff, to review and evaluate the responses using the criteria as provided
in the 2024 NOFA . The panel met on April 2, 2024 and evaluated each response and
formed a preliminary recommendation. The panel did not identify a ne ed for additional
information. A final preliminary evaluation was provided to the panel prior to and after
presenting the recommendation to the City Manager.
Funding Recommendation
Staff’s funding recommendation, in order or priority, for the 202 4 Affordable Housing
NOFA is detailed in Table 2 below. The 2024 NOFA made available approximately $6
million in financial assistance and 50 PBVs. Staff is recommending the conditional
approval of up to two proposals, exceeding the published $6 million available and the 50
PBVs, at the discretion of the City Council.
Funding is recommended from a variety of sources and in alignment with the availability
of funding and to meet the requirements of these sources.
1 Shadow Way Apartments is a previously funded project by the City of Oceanside, which in addition to
the 2024 NOFA request of $1,000,000 will be assuming the current outstanding City loan balance of $4.2

Evaluation
Each request for funding received was evaluated using the criteria provided in the
NOFA. Summaries of the proposals are provided in Attachment 2 . All proposals
demonstrated financial feasibility and developer capacity to provide quality affordable
housing to meet the needs of Oceanside’s lower-income households.
The proposals recommended for funding stood out in several areas, including deeper
affordability targeting of key and varied target population groups, committed funding,
suitability for available funding sources, development teams with a proven track record
in Oceanside and the San Diego region, and provide a pipeline of projects over the next
few years. Justification for Staff’s funding recommendation is provided below.
Coast Villas at 1111 & 1123 South Coast Highway
The Project Sponsor (National Core and San Diego Community Housing Corporation) is
proposing a 56-unit permanent housing development for seniors. The proposal meets a
number of identified special needs groups, such as seniors, persons with disabilities,
extremely low-income households at risk of homelessness, the unhoused and homeless
veterans. Of the 56 units, 34 percent (19 dus) will be dedicated to seniors currently
unhoused or at risk of homelessness and 12 units will be for HUD VASH participants
(see Unit Mix and Income Levels of Attachment 2 ). The remaining 36 units will be
affordable for very low -income households and one unit for the on- site property
manager. With the special needs groups served, S taff recommends funding of the
project to provide for housing opportunities that address various needs within the
community.
As a permanent supportive housing development, the project qualifies under the
provisions of Senate Bill 2162, that allows this type of development as by -right with no
discretionary action by the City, therefore, enhancing the feasibility and readiness of the
project.
The Project Sponsor is preparing to apply for 9 percent Low Income Housing Tax
Credits (LIHTC or tax credits) in the first round of 2025, with an award expected by the
Summer 2025 (see Development Timeline of Attachment 2). With a 2025 application
date for tax credits, Staff recommends the funding of Coast Villas in order to provide a
development pipeline for affordable housing.
The City’s participation in the project , in the form of soft financing, characterized by low
interest rates and repayment from residual cash of the development project, will
improve the project’s competitiveness for LIHTCs, which is highly competitive and often
receives more requests than the funding available. The City’s funding support is
especially important since the project site is located in what is considered a “Low
Resource” area for tax credit funding purposes. The California Tax Credit Allocation
Committee (CTCAC) and State Housing and Community Development (HCD) publish
an Opportunity Map ranking areas throughout the state from the Highest Resource to
Low Resources based upon the characteristics of the areas shown by research to be
associated with positive economic, educational, and health outcomes for low -income
families (e.g., median home value, adult education, employment, etc.).
The County of San Diego is currently in the process of reviewing Coast Villas for its No
Place Like Home (NPLH) funds in the approximate amount of $2 ,471,500. This project
represents the last affordable housing development in the San Diego region to apply for
the remaining available NPLH funds, with the funds to be awarded by mid-June 2024 or
revert back to the State . The a ward of NPLH funds is contingent upon award of the
City’s funding. Additionally, with the pr oject serving 12 homeless veterans and seniors
at extremely low-income, the project is suitable for funding from the City’s $1.9 million in
available HOME-ARP funds that need to be committed for expenditure.
While located in a Low Resource area, the project is a site identified within the City’s
Housing Element for housing to meet the City’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation
(RHNA) for moderate/above- moderate-income households but would provide greater
affordability. The site is within the coastal area of Oceanside, the Townsite
neighborhood, and within Coast Highway Corridor area in close proximity to the Sprinter
station and other neighborhood amenities. The project not only provides much needed
affordable housing for seniors but would serve as a catalyst for smart growth and seek
to revitalize an underutilized auto sales lot within the corridor.
National CORE and SDCHC are both well -established non-profit affordable housing
developers in the San Diego region, with multiple projects in Oceanside (Cape Cod
Senior Villas, La Mision, Mission Cove, and the soon to open Greenbrier Village).
National CORE’s ownership and management experience includes over 9,000
apartment homes in 85 communities, 10 of which are supportive housing serving those
with special needs. SDCHC’s presence is in the San Diego region with over 1,450
rental homes and 85 first time homebuyer opportunities. SDCHC has served as the co -
developer on the Greenbrier Village Apartments in Oceanside with National C ORE, as
well as other more recent projects throughout the San Diego region.
With the project serving deeper affordability levels at 30 percent of the AMI, the project
is well suited to be funded with the City’s HOME -ARP funding or Low/Moderate Income
Housing funds. The balance of financial assistance would be allocated from the City’s
available Inclusionary Housing In -lieu Fee funds. An award of PBVs is necessary to
provide additional operating subsidies to achieve this level of deeper affordability
targeting.
2136 South El Camino Real
The Project Sponsor (Mirka Investments) is proposing a 111- unit mixed income (30 to
80 percent of the Area Median Income) housing development serving large families and
individuals, with 30 units of supportive housing for persons with developmental
disabilities (see Unit Mix and Income Levels of Attachment 2). While the project does
not provide housing for HUD VASH participants (homeless veterans), the project
provides 50 percent of the units (55 dus) as 3-bedrooms, serving larger family sizes and
provides deep affordability targeting with 56 percent of the units for extremely low and
very low -income households. Given the larger family units and serving persons with
developmental disabilities, Staff recommends funding of the project, along with the
Coast Villas senior project, to provide housing opportunities that address various needs
within the community.
As a supportive housing development, the project qualifies under the provisions of
Senate Bill 2162, that allows this type of development as by -right with no discretionary
action by the City, therefore, enhancing the feasibility and readiness of the project.
The Project Sponsor applied for Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds (Bonds) and the
companion 4 percent tax credits on April 23, 2024. Award of 1st round Bonds/4 percent
tax credits will be made on August 3, 2024 (see Development Timeline of Attachment
2). With a 202 4 application date for Bond/ tax credit financing and a by -right entitlement
process, Staff supports funding of the project based upon project readiness and the
ability to bring on line 111 affordable housing units more quickly than the other new
construction proposals.
The City’s participation in the project will improve the project’s competitiveness for
Bonds and 4 percent tax credits . The project is support ed by its competitive location in
the “Highest Resource” area for tax credit funding purposes. T he project is also a site
identified within the City’s Housing Element for housing to meet the City’s Regional
Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) for low-income households.
Mirka Investments is a San Diego based affordable housing developer, with over 50
years collective experience. In its six years, Mirka has brought forward eight
development projects totaling 467 units to the Southern California region. In the next
two to five years, Mirka has a development pipeline of 20 projects totaling nearly 2,200
units. One such project is the 43- unit affordable housing development in Oceanside,
known as South River Village, breaking ground by Summer 2024.
With the project serving deeper affordability levels at 30 percent of the AMI, the project
is also well suited to be funded with the City’s LMIHF . The balance of financial
assistance would be allocated from the City’s available Inclusionary Housing In-lieu Fee
funds. An award of PBVs is necessary to provide additional operating subsidies to
achieve this level of deeper affordability targeting.
Waitlist
At this time, Staff is recommending that the remaining proposals (Olive Park, Pierview
Way, and Shadow Way) be placed on a waiting list for City funding should the
recommended proposals not move forward. A ll proposals demonstrated consistency
with the housing goals of the City as outlined within its Housing Element and
Consolidated Plan, expedited deployment of NOFA funds achieving occupancy within
three years or less, leveraging of other resources and reasonable costs for affordable
housing, and proposed by capable and experienced teams.
Financing Structure/Terms
Financing and development of affordable housing is generally proposed as joint private-
public partnerships. With rents restricted at the affordable levels, particularly for
extremely low-income households, for the 55-year time period, the net operating income
is insufficient to support a loan large enough to cover all the project costs.
Affordable housing projects f inance a significant portion of the development costs
through the use of 9 percent tax credits or Bonds with the companion 4 percent tax
credits. To close the financing gap, projects seek other forms of financial assistance,
such as funding from other local public agencies or the deferral of a portion of their
developer fee . A summary of the t otal development costs and sources and uses of
funds are provided in Attachment 2.
Funding Sources
Financial assistance is recommended primarily from the City’s Inclusionary Housing In-
lieu Fee fund for both proposals (Coast Villas and El Camino Real). The available fund
balance is approximately $14 million.
Staff proposes the use of HOME -ARP funds for Coast Villas. In accordance with HUD
requirements for HOME -ARP, the City must commit these funds to a housing project
serving the homeless or those at risk of homelessness. F unding of the available
HOME-ARP balance of approximately $2 million to the Coast Villas project would assist
the City in meeting the HUD requirement of qualifying populations to be served.
